deep.reconstruction:
Context: This is folio 16 of the Latin prize essay that Riemann submitted to the Paris Academy in 1861 on heat conduction (the 'Commentatio mathematica, qua respondere tentatur quaestioni ab Ill.ma Academia Parisiensi propositae'). It was printed posthumously in his Werke (1876, ed. Weber and Dedekind). The previous page set up the problem. The heat equation in a body with conductivity tensor b is rewritten through new variables s_i. The question then becomes when the quadratic form Σ b_{ιι'} ds_ι ds_{ι'} can be transformed into one with constant coefficients. The four-index expression (ιι',ι''ι''') is the Riemann curvature tensor in Riemann's normalization. Expression (II) is Σ(ιι',ι''ι''') p^{ιι'} p^{ι''ι'''}, where p^{ab} = ds_a δs_b − ds_b δs_a are the bivector (Plücker) components. Expression (III) is −½ (II) divided by the Gram determinant |ds|²|δs|² − (ds·δs)².

(1) Geometric interpretation (top of page, completing a sentence from p.15).
- Treat sqrt(Σ b ds ds) as the line element of an n-dimensional space.
- From the point s, draw all geodesics whose initial directions are proportional to α ds + β δs, for arbitrary α and β. These form a 2-dimensional surface.
- That surface can be developed into ordinary 3-space (as an abstract 2-manifold with its induced metric).
- Expression (III) is then the curvature measure (Gaussian curvature) of this surface at the point s. The footnote mark (1) refers to a note elsewhere.
- In modern terms: (III) is the sectional curvature K(σ) of the 2-plane σ = span(ds, δs), i.e. K = R(X,Y,Y,X)/(|X|²|Y|² − ⟨X,Y⟩²). It equals the Gaussian curvature at p of the surface exp_p(σ).
- The invariance claimed on p.15 is consistent with this. Under ds → α ds + β δs, δs → γ ds + δ δs, every p^{ab} is multiplied by (αδ − βγ), so numerator and denominator both scale by (αδ − βγ)².

(2) The case n = 3.
- The bivector space Λ²R³ is 3-dimensional, with coordinates p^{23}, p^{31}, p^{12}.
- So (II) is a quadratic form in these three quantities, with a symmetric 3×3 coefficient matrix. That gives 6 coefficients.
- Requiring (II) to vanish identically gives six PDEs for the six functions b_{ιι'}. These are R_{abcd} = 0; in 3D this is equivalent to Ric = 0, i.e. the six components of the Ricci/Einstein tensor vanishing.
- These are necessary (shown on p.15) for the metric to be flat, i.e. reducible to constant coefficients.
- Riemann states that it is 'not difficult, by the notions just given' to show they are also sufficient. He does not prove it here; the sufficiency argument was sketched earlier in the essay via the maximum/minimum characterisation and the geodesic construction.
- He adds that only three of the six are independent of one another. The most natural reading (my interpretation, not stated in the text) is that the six equations satisfy three differential identities: the contracted Bianchi identity ∇^a G_{ab} = 0. Equivalently, a 3-metric has 6 components minus 3 coordinate freedoms, leaving 3 essential functions. The equations are not algebraically dependent.

(3) Application to the prize question.
- To answer the Academy's question, one would substitute into these six equations the forms of b found earlier by the method already explained (b expressed through the temperature level functions).
- This would yield all cases in which the temperature u in a homogeneous body can depend only on time and two spatial variables.
- Riemann says lack of time prevented him from carrying out these calculations. He will only list the solutions.
- He restricts, for brevity, to the simplest case: the isotropic heat equation (I) u_{x1x1} + u_{x2x2} + u_{x3x3} = a² u_t. He says the other cases reduce to it; the enumeration continues on the next page (cases m = 1..4).
errors: No mathematical error on the page.
The sufficiency of the six conditions is asserted ('nec difficile ... est demonstratu') without proof on this page.

The independence claim ('ternas tantum esse a se independentes') is stated without explanation. Read literally as algebraic independence it would be false: the six components of the 3D curvature tensor are algebraically independent. It is correct only if read as differential dependence (via the Bianchi identities) or as a count of essential functions modulo coordinate changes.

The calculations needed to answer the prize question are explicitly left undone. Riemann admits this ('angustia temporis non permisit'), and this incompleteness is one reason the essay did not receive the prize.

results.what: Curvature expression (III) interpreted as the Gaussian curvature of the surface swept out by geodesics tangent to the 2-plane spanned by ds and δs
In n = 3, the curvature form is a quadratic form in the 3 bivector components, giving 6 conditions for flatness; these six conditions suffice
results.modern_name: Vanishing of the Riemann tensor (equivalently the Ricci tensor in 3D) as necessary and sufficient for local flatness

results.what: Of the six flatness equations, only three are independent
results.modern_name: Differential dependence via the (contracted) Bianchi identities / count of 3 essential functions in a 3-metric
results.usually_credited_to: Bianchi identities: Voss 1880, Ricci, Bianchi 1902; the remark itself is in Riemann's Commentatio (Werke 1876)

results.what: Programme to classify heat flows depending on time and only two spatial variables by inserting the conductivity forms into the flatness conditions
results.modern_name: Application of flatness conditions to the Paris prize problem on isothermal surfaces in heat conduction

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay, published in his collected Werke in 1876 and extensively discussed (Weber, Dedekind, Farwell–Knee, Laugwitz). The sectional-curvature interpretation and the n=3 flatness conditions are well known as his. The cryptic remark that only three of the six conditions are independent is a known foreshadowing of the Bianchi identities, so it is not new.

checkable.asserts: Under ds -> α ds + β δs, δs -> γ ds + δ δs, the bivector components ds_i δs_j - ds_j δs_i scale by (αδ - βγ). Hence (III), a ratio of two forms each quadratic in these components, is invariant (should return the zero vector).
The Gaussian curvature of the geodesic polar metric dr^2 + sin(r)^2 dphi^2 is 1. This illustrates the curvature of a surface spanned by geodesics from a point.
For n=3 the bivector space has dimension 3, so a symmetric quadratic form on it has 6 coefficients: six flatness equations.
A 3-dimensional metric has 6 components minus 3 coordinate freedoms, i.e. 3 essential functions. This is consistent with 'only three independent' read as differential (Bianchi) dependence.
